findings.control_name: SSE-C Must Be Disabled on S3 Buckets
findings.control_description: S3 buckets must have SSE-C (server-side encryption with customer-provided keys) disabled. SSE-C allows any principal with s3:PutObject to encrypt objects with an externally-held key that AWS never stores. Ransomware syndicates use this to encrypt data without needing KMS access — the data is irrecoverable without the attacker's key. Unlike BYOKM ransomware (CTL.KMS.ENTROPY.EXTERNAL.ORIGIN.001), SSE-C requires no KMS permissions and bypasses all SCP controls on kms:ImportKeyMaterial. AWS began disabling SSE-C by default for new buckets in April 2026. Technique documented by Farris, extended from the BYOKM ransomware kill chain.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 120 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-10T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Bucket allows SSE-C uploads. Any principal with s3:PutObject can encrypt objects with an externally-held key, enabling ransomware without KMS involvement.
remediation.action: Disable SSE-C on the bucket. As of April 2026, AWS disables SSE-C by default for new buckets and existing buckets in accounts without SSE-C-encrypted data. For buckets that still allow SSE-C, disable it via the S3 console or API. Verify existing objects are not SSE-C-encrypted before disabling.

near_miss_chains.description: S3-native ransomware via SSE-C: buckets allow customer-provided encryption keys AND lack ransomware resilience controls (versioning, Object Lock). An attacker with s3:PutObject encrypts objects using SSE-C with a key only they hold. Unlike BYOKM ransomware (byokm_ransomware_kill_chain), SSE-C requires no KMS permissions, bypasses all SCP controls on KMS actions, and the encryption key never exists in AWS systems — no court order or AWS intervention can recover the data. The only defense is disabling SSE-C (available since April 2026) and ensuring versioning/Object Lock preserves pre-encryption copies. Technique documented by Farris as the S3-native companion to the BYOKM kill chain.

findings.control_name: S3 Access Log Destination Must Be in Same Account or Org
findings.control_description: When S3 server access logging is enabled, the log destination bucket must be in the same account or organization. An attacker can redirect access logs to their own bucket, capturing every S3 request path — which may contain sensitive data in query strings and object keys. Technique: hackingthe.cloud S3 server access logs exfiltration.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 120 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-10T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: S3 access log destination is in an external account. Request paths and metadata are being sent outside the organization.
remediation.action: Change the access log destination to a bucket in the same account or organization. Investigate whether the external destination was intentionally configured.

findings.control_name: S3 Object Ownership Must Be Bucket Owner Enforced
findings.control_description: S3 buckets must have Object Ownership set to BucketOwnerEnforced, which disables ACLs entirely. When ACLs are disabled, the bucket owner automatically owns every object regardless of who uploaded it, and access is controlled exclusively through IAM and bucket policies. This eliminates the entire class of ACL-based exposure: public grants, privilege escalation via WRITE_ACP, and object-level ACL overrides. Since April 2023 new buckets default to BucketOwnerEnforced, but buckets created before this date may still have ACLs enabled.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 120 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-10T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Bucket does not have Object Ownership set to BucketOwnerEnforced. ACLs remain active and can grant public or cross-account access to individual objects, bypassing bucket policies.
remediation.action: Set Object Ownership to BucketOwnerEnforced using aws s3api put-bucket-ownership-controls. This disables all ACLs on the bucket. Before enabling, audit existing ACL grants and migrate any legitimate access to bucket policies or IAM policies. All existing ACL-based access will stop working once BucketOwnerEnforced is set.

fix_plan.action: Set Object Ownership to BucketOwnerEnforced using aws s3api put-bucket-ownership-controls. This disables all ACLs on the bucket. Before enabling, audit existing ACL grants and migrate any legitimate access to bucket policies or IAM policies. All existing ACL-based access will stop working once BucketOwnerEnforced is set.

findings.control_name: S3 Bucket Must Abort Incomplete Multipart Uploads
findings.control_description: S3 bucket has no lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads. An attacker who can initiate uploads (s3:PutObject) can start millions of multipart uploads and never complete them. The incomplete parts accumulate storage costs indefinitely — there is no automatic cleanup. This is a denial-of-wallet vector: the attacker pays nothing (no completed objects), the bucket owner pays for every stored part. A lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload and a short DaysAfterInitiation threshold (e.g. 7 days) limits exposure.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 120 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-10T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Bucket has no lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads. Incomplete parts accumulate indefinitely and incur storage costs.
remediation.action: Add a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload set to a short DaysAfterInitiation threshold (7 days is typical). Apply to the entire bucket (no prefix filter) to ensure all incomplete uploads are cleaned up.

marker_findings.control_description: Fact-recording marker for S3 buckets tagged data-classification=phi. Emits an informational finding (NOT a violation) on every PHI-tagged bucket so cross-resource chains can compose it with violation findings on related identities or resources. Examples: a Cognito unauth role with s3:GetObject targeting a PHI bucket; an IAM role outside the covered entity that can AssumeRole to a principal that reaches a PHI bucket. PHI tagging on its own is the desired state — never a finding to triage. The marker exists so the chain engine can join "violation on the access side" with "data classification on the storage side" without forcing the collector to denormalise every join shape into a per-asset boolean.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 120 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-10T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: No remediation. PHI tagging is the desired state.
remediation.action: None. This marker exists as a chain-detection ingredient. To suppress noise on dashboards, filter findings by control_id when rendering Findings — markers should appear in a separate "facts" panel rather than the violation list.

near_miss_chains.description: Bedrock knowledge base indexes an S3 bucket AND that bucket carries the data-classification=phi marker. RAG retrieval through the agent connected to this knowledge base returns PHI to whoever queries the agent. Same compound shape as cognito_unauth_phi_s3 but on the AI-data axis: each side is a fact-recording marker (KB indexes bucket X; bucket X is PHI), neither a violation alone — the dangerous combination is the join on a shared bucket ARN. The Bedrock side stamps target_bucket_arn on the knowledge base; the S3 side's scope is its own ARN (asset.ID), which the resolver returns when the property path is absent on the storage asset.

Cognito identity pool admits anonymous AWS credentials AND its unauthenticated role carries S3 actions AND the action target is an S3 bucket tagged data-classification=phi. The compound describes an internet-to-PHI data path that no individual control catches: UNAUTH.S3 alone fires on any S3 access (over-broad signal); the PHI marker alone is the desired state. Their conjunction over a shared bucket ARN — surfaced via scope_field on the bucket's identity — is the HIPAA-reportable shape.
